RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Secondary Education, and reforms therein, are primarily the 
responsibility of the State Governments. The Mid-term Appraisal of the 10th 
Five Year Plan has, inter-alia, recommended that "in order to plan for a major 
expansion of Secondary Education in the event of achievement of full or near full 
retention under SSA (Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan), setting up a new mission for 
Secondary Education, on the lines of SSA, should be considered". 
A Committee of the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) was 
constituted in September 2004, to prepare a blueprint for Universalisation of 
Secondary Education consequent upon the attainment of Universalisation of 
Elementary Education. The Committee submitted its Report in June, 2005. 
The above recommendations are being examined in consultation with 
concerned agencies, after which a scheme may emerge for implementation 
during the XI Plan.

SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, the expert agencies concerned with 
the secondary education would be the NCERT for the curriculum, the CBSE 
for the examination reforms and the NC TE for the teachers' training and the 
NIOS for the open and distan ce education. And, at the State level, Sir, it is 
SCERT, the State Boards of Secondary Education, State open schools, 
wherever they exist. 
And, Sir, when it comes to the refo rms, the reforms are basically the 
qualitative and the quantitative. When we look at the quantitative reforms we 
have the universalising access to the secondary education, and this would imply 
that every child in the relevant age group should have access to secondary 
education and this means that the schools should be within the reachable distance 
to the child. It can be within 5-7 kilometres. It also incorporates enhancing the 
participation rate. Presently, forty per cent of the children today between the age 
groups of 14-18 years are enrolled in classes 9-12 and this is definitely a very 
dismal percentage to look at, and this needs to be substantially enhanced and 
definitely the reforms are being steered into this direction. 
Coming to the qualitative reforms, Sir, we are working on the 
improvement of quality, and this implies the improvement in curriculum, 
examination system, teaching methods, tr aining of teachers, availability of 
infrastructure like classrooms, etc.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The Central Government considered the various recommendations/ 
proposals relating to State funding of elections received by it. With a view to 
building consensus among the recognized political parties, it has decided to 
request the Election Commission of India for its consideration certain 
recommendations. Accordingly, on the 2 nd January, 2006, the Government 
requested the Election Commission of India to recommend, in consultation with 
the recognized political parties, the quantities of the following items to be 
provided to the recognized political parties or to the

Asim Azmi.

candidates set up by them taking into consideration the geographical features 
and means of communication available:- 
"(a) For recognized political parties: 
(i)    Suitable rent-free accommodation for its headquarters. 
(ii) One rent-free telephone, with Subscriber Trunk Dialing facility with 
a specified number of telephone calls over and above the free 
calls permitted to any subscriber. 
(iii) the amount of time to be distributed on private cable television 
network and electronic media. 
(b) For candidates of recognized Parties: 
(i)    Specified quantity of petrol/diesel. 
(ii)    Specified quantity of paper for printing. 
(iii)    Postal stamps of a certain specified amount. 
(iv) For an assembly election, one set of loudspeakers and for a 
parliamentary election, one se t of loudspeakers for every 
assembly segment, subject to a maximum of six such sets. 
(v) For an assembly election, one te lephone with a specified number of 
free calls, and for a parliamentary election, at the rate of one 
telephone for every assembly segment, subject to a maximum of six 
telephones. 
(vi) On the day of poll, some minimum arrangements may be made for the 
candidates' camps at each polling station. 
(vii) Supply of refreshments and food packets to the counting agents 
inside the counting hall." 
A reply from the Election Commission is awaited. 
2. The Government also decided that the Central and the State

(a) whether it is a fact that the Supreme Court has ruled that courts can extend the 
time limit of ninety days fixed under the Code of Civil Procedure for filing a written 
statement in civil disputes; 
(b) if so, whether it would not lead to further raising the huge arrears of civil cases in 
the country; and 
(c) the number of civil cases pending in District and High Courts as on the 31st 
December, 2005 and details of Government's plan to liquidate these arrears? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati 
Mohsina Kidwai. 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
Statement 
Extension of time limit for filing written statement in civil disputes 
The Supreme Court in Kailash versus Nanhku and Others (2005) 4 SCC 480, 
Vol. Ill ruled that Order 8 rule 1, proviso as amended by the Code of Civil 
Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002 is directory in character and not mandatory. The 
court further held that though these provisions cast an obligation on defendant to file a 
written statement within the time prescribed therein, the provisions do not deal with nor 
specifically take away the power of the court to take a written statement on record, though 
filed beyond the time as provided for therein. In addition, section 5 of the Limitation 
Act, 1963 enables the Civil Courts to extend the time limit provided under the Code 
of Civil Procedure for filing a suit, written statement, application or appeal if the 
person was prevented by sufficient reason from filing the same within the time 
prescribed. The Supreme Court has held that it is a settled situation in law, the civil 
courts have power to extend the time limit in the cases where the applicant or appellant was 
prevented by sufficient cause to bring his application or appeal or written statement 
within the prescribed time. 
No Direct link between the extension of time and arrears 
There is no direct link between extension of time by the Civil Court by virtue of 
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and increase in the arrears of civil cases. On the 
other hand, when a civil court refuses to extend the time limit prescribed for filing 
written statement, application or appeal, the aggrieved person approaches the appellate 
court against such an order of refusal which adds to the arrears of the civil cases. It 
seems highly just and proper for the civil courts to extend the time limit a case when 
the person was prevented by sufficient reason from filing his case within the 
prescribed time. 
Measures taken by Government to liquidate the arrears 
In High Court 34.24 lakh cases are pending and 254.06 lakh cases are pending 
in the District and Subordinate Courts as on 31.12.2005. In order to reduce pendency of 
cases government has initiated a number of measures which include timely filing the 
vacancies of judges, increasing the judge strength, grouping of cases, involving 
common questions of law, constitution of specialized benches, organizing Lok Adalats at 
regular 
24 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
intervals encouraging alternative modes of dispute resolution like negotiation, 
mediation and arbitration and setting up of special tribunals like Central Administrative 
Tribunals, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family 
Courts and Labour Courts. Further it has been decided to focus on reform in a few core areas 
which include computerization of judiciary, disposal through fast track courts, 
development of physical infrastructure and evolution of strategies to cope with massive 
governance related inadequacies in judicial process through studies, pilots and reform 
projects. The Government has extended the term of existing 1562 Fast Track Courts for 
another five years i.e. upto 31.3.2010 for clearing huge pendency of cases at District 
level.

Vacant Posts of Judges in High Courts 
*34. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the total number of vacancies in the High Courts as on date; 
(b) the steps being taken to fill up the vacancies; 
(c) whether any proposal exists to increase the strength of judges in any of 
the High Courts; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof alongwith the action takes so far? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) to (d) Against the sanctioned strength of 675 Judges in 21 High Courts, 553 
Judges were in position as on 15.2.2006, leaving 122 vacancies to be filled up. 
Filling up of vacancies in the High C ourts is a continuous consultative 
process among the constitutional authorities. While every effort is made to fill 
up the existing vacancies expeditiously, vacancies do keep arising on account of 
retirements, resignation or elevation of Judges. 
After the Supreme Court Judgement of October 6, 1993 in the Supreme 
Court Advocates-on-Record & Anr. Vs. Union of India, read with the 
Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998, the entire process of initiation of 
proposal for appointment of a Judge of a High Court lies with the Chief 
Justice of that High Court Government has been periodically reminding the 
Chief Justices of the High Courts and the Chief Ministers of the States to 
initiate proposals for filling up all vacant posts of judges in the High Courts as 
also those which will be falling vacant during the next six months. 
The judge strength of the High Courts is reviewed every three years. For 
review of Judge strength, the average institution and the pendency of main 
cases during the last five years is co nsidered by taking into account the 
national average or the average rate of disposal of main cases per Judge per 
year in that High Court, whichever is higher. If the disposal per Judge in the 
concerned High Court is below even the national average then instead of 
increasing the strength, the concerned 
42 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
High Court is required to take steps for improvement in the rate of disposal 
of cases. If the average disposal of concerned High Court is above the 
national average then increase in Judge strength is accordingly considered. 
The strength of Additional Judges is reviewed only if there is an increase in 
the arrears of the pending cases during the last 5 years and the disposal per 
Judge is above the national average. The last review was undertaken in the year 
2003 when 94 new posts were recommended. As an interim review, 4 posts 
of Judges were approved for the Bombay High Court in 2005, making the 
total for increase of 98 posts. The next review is due in 2006 for which the 
High Courts have been requested to furnish data.

The scheme envisages provision of a cooked mid-day meal with minimum 
of 300 calories & 8-12 grams of protein. The Central assistance is provided for 
the following main components:— 
(i) Supply of foodgrains (rice/wheat) @ 100 grams per child per 
school day from the nearest FCI godown, 
(ii) Reimbursement of actual cost incurred on transportation of 
foodgrains subject to a ceiling of Rs. 100 per Quintal for Special 
Category States and Rs. 75 per Quintal for others, 
(iii) Assistance for meeting cooking cost @ Re. 1 per child per school 
day, 
(iv) Assistance for provision of mid-day meal during summer 
vacations in drought-affected areas. 
The programme is being implemented in decentralized manner with the 
involvement of local level agencies such as Village Panchayats, Village 
Education Committees, School Management Committees, Parent Teacher 
Associations etc. Women Self-Help Groups/Cooks, particularly, women 
from SC/ST community, are being engaged for cooking the meal.

Statement 
Details of steps taken by the Government to implement the guidelines 
laid down by the Supreme Court and to create awareness about the 
issue of sexual harassment at workplace 
• The Government has requested all the Central Ministries/Departments, Chief 
Secretaries of all the State Governme nts/Union Territory Administrations, 
Universities/Institutions, Central Board of Secondary Education, All India 
Council of Technical Education to constitute complaints committees and to 
ensure that the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court in the Vishaka 
case for prevention of sexual harassment at workplace are implemented. 
• The National Commission for Women (NCW) formulated a Code of 
Conduct for Workplace, putting down the Supreme Court's guidelines 
mentioned above in a simple manner. This has been circulated to State 
Commission for Women, Non-Governmental Organisations, the apex bodies 
of the Corporate Sector, Public Sector Undertakings, Media, 
Ministries/Departments and other institutions. 
• The NCW has instituted a series of interactive meetings with Public Sector 
Undertakings/Banks/Universities/Educational Institutions/ 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
Hotels/Media etc. to assess the extent of implementation of the guidelines. 
• Department of Public Enterprises issued circular in May, 1998 to all 
administrative Ministries/Departments concerned with Central Public Sector 
Establishments to direct the Chief Executives of CPSEs under their 
administrative control for adheren ce and compliance of the Supreme 
Court's guidelines on prevention of sexual harassment by making 
amendments in the CDA Rules of the CPSEs. 
• A Central Committee headed by Secr etary, Department of Women and 
Child Development has been constituted in the Department of Women and 
Child Development to review the implementation of the guidelines. During 
the year 2004, the Committee met on 27-7-2004. In pursuance of the 
meeting, all Ministries/Departm ents and State Governments/UT 
Administrations were again requested to ensure setting up of complaints 
committee and to ensure its proper functioning. 
• So far as implementation of the Supreme Court guidelines in regard to 
setting up of complaint committee in small establishments like shops and call 
centres are concerned, section 1(3) of the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1947 applies to every establishment wherein 100 and more 
workers are employed. However, appropriate Government may apply the 
provisions of the Act to any industrial establishment employing less than 
100 persons. Since the State Governments are the appropriate Government 
in respect of commercial establis hments like shops and call centres, 
necessary. instruction have been issued by the Ministry of Labour and 
Employment during January, 2005 to all Labour Secretaries asking them to 
suitable action to apply the provisions of the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946 to small establishments like call centres and 
shops in the unorganised sector. 
• The Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 have been amended to 
include sexual harassment as a misconduct. The Central Civil Services 
(Control, Classification and Appeal) Rules, 1965 have been amended during 
July, 2004 to provide that the complaints Committee

inquiry into disciplinary proceedings for award of a major penalty).

1946 so that the sexual harassment of women at workplace in the private sector

exports 
1. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to 
the Information Technology Sector, with the exception of 
Business-to-consumer (B2C ) e-commerce are under the

and Peripheral is zero %. Excise duty on computers is zero %.

ROM Drives continue to be exempt from excise duty.

goods on payment of 5% customs duty. The Export Obligation

†112.    DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
(a) whether Government's attention have been drawn towards the Annual 
Status of Education Report; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that as per this report the condition of school 
education is very pitiable; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government have taken any steps to improve the standard of 
school education; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (e) 
The findings of the Annual Survey of Education Report (ASER) are not much 
at variance with the Government's own data-base and information. The 
available data for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) indicates that the number 
of out of school children has reduced from 320 lakhs in 2001-02 to 134 lakhs in 
2005-06, in the 6-14 years age group. This has been confirmed by a national 
survey commissioned by the Govt, of India through an independent agency, Social 
& Rural Research Institute-Indian Market Research Bureau (SRI-IMRB) during 
July-October 2005. 
The drop out rate at the primary stage has reduced from 39.03% in 2001-02 
to 31.36% in 2003-04. The reduction in the drop out rate for girls is significantly 
better, where it has come down by 11 percentage points in the same period. 
Under SSA, the investment in school infrastructure has been steadily 
increasing over the years. 1.29 lakh new schools have been opened, 1.06 lakh 
schools buildings and 2.98 lakh additional class rooms have been constructed 
or are near completion. 
The National Council for Educational Research & Training (NCERT) 
undertakes countrywide sample surveys on student achievement levels for 
particular classes regularly. The recently completed achievement survey for 
Class-V has indicated mean achievement levels of 46.7% in Mathematics and 
58.3% in Language. 
Under SSA, several activities are undertaken to improve the quality of 
elementary education with a view to increase the learning achievement levels 
of students in government schools. This includes 
82 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
recruitment of 4.92 lakh additional teachers to improve the pupil teacher 
ratio, in service training of about 30 lakh teachers for a period of 20 days 
each year, free distribution of text books for primary and upper primary 
classes to about 5.02 crore SC, ST and girl students, regular academic 
support to primary and upper primary schools through 7422 Block Resource 
Centres and 70735 Cluster Resource Centres, regular evaluation of students 
and monitoring of school performance.

102 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to 
(e) The findings of the Annual Survey of Education Report (ASER)! are not much at 
variance with the Government's own data-base and information. The available data 
for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) indicates that the number of out of school 
children has reduced from 320 lakhs in 2001-02, to 134 lakhs in 2005-06 in the 6-14 
years age group. This has been confirmed by a national survey commissioned by the Govt, 
of India through an independent agency, Social and Rural Research Institute-Indian 
Market Research Bureau (SRI-IMRB) during July—October 2005. 
The drop out rate at the primary stage has reduced from 39.03% in 2001-02 
to 31 36% in 2003-04. The reduction in the drop out rate for girls is significantly 
better, where it has come down by 11 percentage points in the same period. 
Under SSA, the investment in school infrastructure has been steadily 
increasing over the years. 1.29 lakh new schools have been opened, 1.06 lakh 
schools buildings and 2.98 lakh additional class rooms have been constructed 
or are near completion. State wise details are given in the Statement (See 
below). 
The ASER report does no provide data on schools without roofs 
The National Council for Educational Research & Training (NCERT) 
undertakes countrywide sample surveys on student achievement levels for 
particular classes regularly. The recently completed achievement survey for 
Class—V has indicated mean achievement levels of 46.7% in Mathematics and 
58.3% in Language. 
Under SSA, several activities are under taken to improve the quality of 
elementary education with a view to increase the learning achievement levels 
of students in government schools. This includes recruitment of 4.92 lakh 
additional teachers to improve the pupil teacher ratio, in service training of about 
30 lakh teachers for a period of 20 days each year, free distribution of text books 
for primary and upper primary classes to about 5 02 crore SC, ST and girl 
students, regular academic support to primary and upper primary schools 
through 7422 Block Resource Centres and 70735 Cluster Reserve Centres, 
regular evaluation of students and monitoring of school performance.

matters or financial matters, or transfe rring the cases that are more than five

(c) and (d) The Central Government has been periodically monitoring the 
pendency position in various courts. The steps taken for speedy disposal of pending 
cases, include timely filling the vacancies of judges, increasing the judge strength, 
grouping of cases involving common questions of law, constitution of 
specialized benches, organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals, encouraging 
alternative modes of dispute resolution like negotiation, mediation and 
arbitration and setting up of special tribunals like Central Administrative 
Tribunals, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tri bunals, 
Family Courts, Labour Courts etc. The Central Govt, has also extended the life 
of 1562 Fast Track Courts in march 2005 till March 2010 to clear long pending 
sessions cases. 
The judge strength of the High Courts is reviewed every three years. For 
review of judge strength, the average institution and the pendency of main cases 
during the last five years is considered by taking into account the national average 
or the average rate of disposal of main cases per judge per year in the High 
Court whichever is higher. If the disposal per judge in the concerned High 
court is below even the national average then instead of increase the strength, the 
concerned High Corut is required to take steps for improvement in the rate of 
disposal of cases. If the average disposal of concerned High Court is above the 
national average then increase in Judge strength is accordingly considered. The 
strength of Additional judges is reviewed only if there is an increase in the arrears 
of the pending cases during the last 5 years and the disposal per judge is above the 
national average.

Statement-I 
Small Industry Cluster Development Programme (SICDP) (Formerly Known 
as UPTEC) 
1. Objectives 
A Scheme on Technology Upgradation and Management Programme, called 
UPTEC, was launched in February, 1998, to address the issues related to 
technology upgradation and modernisation of small scale industries in 
clusters. The Scheme has been renamed, in 2003-04, as Small Industry 
Cluster Development Programme with the objective of holistic cluster 
development. 
2. Salient Features 
(i) The Scheme provides Central Grants to State Governments and 
other eligible organisations for taking up diagnostic study, 
resourcing of technology, facilitating transfer of technology from 
producer to end user, setting up demonstration plants, R&D 
activities, etc. and organising workshops, seminars, training and 
study visits for quicker diffussion of improved technology and 
management across the cluster of small enterprises. 
(ii) The Scheme aims at fac ilitating technology upgradation, 
improvement of productivity, energy conservation, pollution 
control, product diversification, skill building, etc., so that the 
cluster as a whole becomes more competitive and viable.

Child labour and protection of children's rights 
182. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a group of 150 children participating in the third 
National Bal Mitra Mahapanchayata at Viratnagar in Rajasthan have demanded 
an end to child labour and protection of their rights to get education and 
equal opportunities; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) action Government propose to take to address these issues? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND 
CHILD DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RENUKA CHOWDHURY). (a) 
Government is not aware of such Bal Mitra Mahapanchayata. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The problem of child labour requires to be dealt through sustained efforts 
and the Government is committed to the goal of elimination of child labour in 
all its forms. Considering the nature and magnitude of the problem, a gradual and 
sequential approach has been adopted to withdraw and rehabilitate child labour 
beginning with the children workin g in the hazardous occupations and 
processes. The action plan adopted by the Government to eliminate child labour 
comprises of legislative measures, general development programmes for 
benefiting children and a project based action plan in areas of high 
concentration of child labour. Unde r the NCLP Scheme, the children are 
withdrawn from work and put into special schools. They are provided basic 
education, vocational training, mid-day meal and health check up in order to 
prepare them to be mainstreamed into  formal schooling system. As of now, 
the scheme is being implemented in 250 districts.

Minister 30 yeas ago. The rural health delivery system is still most unsatisfactory. 
It needs a special thrust. Just yesterday or day before, I raised the question 
before the Minister as to why our doctor s are not going to the rural areas, and 
whether we are having a programme for paramedicos to go into the rural 
areas. We have got to meet the threat that the rural population faces. The evil of 
female infanticide, for example, is a shame and disgrace on this country. 
Nutritional inputs have to be given. Children are being born, stunted in body 
and mind, because they do not get nutritional inputs either through the nursing 
mothers or through the pregnant mothers, and we have to give these services 
as far as possible in the rural areas. I would suggest that the Government must 
seriously consider this aspect. We must launch a massive programme of 
contraceptive technology to ensure population stab ilization. The House knows 
that our rate of growth is still 1.7 per cent, which m eans that we are adding 
virtually one Australia every year to the population of India. If you are going to get 
rid of poverty, unless we move towards population stabilization, that is not 
possible, and that can only be ensured by empowering the women, by giving 
them the choice of contraceptive and by providing contraceptive technology, 
particularly, in the rural areas. 
Also, Sir, a massive condom programme needs to be launched to save us 
from the scourge of AIDS. AIDS is bec oming a very major problem. We are 
the Second Largest Country in the World, having the second largest number of 
HIV AIDS' patients after South Africa. This is an explosion waiting to occur, 
and unless we take this contraceptive technology to the people, to the villages, 
we are going to find one day, within the next 5-10 years, that there is going to be 
a massive explosion 
190 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
of AIDS that can decimate our population, that can destroy, particularly, the 
weaker sections of the society, and that will cause havoc in the country. Therefore, I 
would like to see that the Rural Health  Mission does not only concentrate on 
health, but also concentrates on population stabilization, family planning and 
AIDS control. I understand that Brazil, which is also very much like us, a large 
country with huge areas and population, 95 per cent of its population is 
protected from AIDS, whereas, we are far behind, I suggest that this is 
something to which the entire House has got to give special consideration. 
That is the third thing. We have t he Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme, we 
have the Bharat Nirman, we have the National Rural Health Scheme. 
Then, there is the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission. Our 
slums are proliferating. Wherever you travel in India, whether they are big cities 
or small cities, the slums are proliferating. And if you look at the satellite 
photographs of India, you will see them spreading like cancerous growth 
throughout the length and breadth of this country. Now, unless our urban 
conglomerates also have some kind of validity and viability, chaos is going to 
exist. It is estimated that within an other ten years, 50 per cent of our 
population is going to be living in the urban areas and, therefore, these 63 
towns, that have been chosen by the Government, need special consideration. 
Transportation is a major block. Delhi Metro shows that is can be done. Kolkata 
Metro is already there. We need to have innovative solutions to these 
problems in the cities; otherwise, our cities are becoming totally unmanageable, 
ungovernable. Therefore, in the slum areas we have all sorts of tensions growing, 
which are not conducive towards a harmonious society. 
And, then, you have the fifth pillar in the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. Sir, the 
House will agree with me that it is a matter of shame and disgrace that 60 years 
after independence, we still have crores and crores of people in this country, who 
are illiterate. Although the percentage of illiteracy has, certainly dropped, the 
total number are still very large and, therefore, we have to ensure the Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan. This will involve massive building programmes for schools, 
massive employment opportunities for teachers. Unemployment is one of the 
biggest problems we are facing. Through the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, through 
the building of school structures and the teachers' appointment, you can go a 
long way to meet the problem of unemployment.

Influenza Virus (H5n1) 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULT URE AND THE MINISTER OF 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI 
SHARAD PAWAR): Sir, large scale death of poultry had been reported from 
navapur Taluka of District Nandurbar, Ma harashtra. Preliminary investigations 
had indicated the possibility of Newcastle (Ranikhet) disease. Samples were 
also sent to High Security Animal Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal, to test 
for Avian Influenza. 
The samples have since been tested at High Security Animal Disease 
Laboratory, Bhopal. Test reports confirm that samples are positive for H5N1 
strain of Avian Influenza in poultry at Navapur, District Nandurbar, Maharashtra. 
A series of strategic actions hav e been initiated immediately on 
confirmation of Avian Influenza. 
[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair.] 
These actions include declaration of infected and surveillance areas, 
absolute ban on movement of poultry or its products in infected areas, closure 
of poultry and egg markets and shops in infected areas, 
246 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
5.00 P.M. 
destruction of attected poultry followed by proper disposal, etc. The 
Government of India has rushed to Maharashtra vaccines for poultry, Tamiflu 
for humans and personal protective equipment. Rapid Response Teams of 
the Department of Animal Husbandry, Da irying and Fisheries and Ministry of 
Health & Family Welfare have been ru shed to the affected areas. The teams 
of the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare are carrying out surveillance of 
human population in the area. 
It is the policy of the Government to compensate for loss of poultry on 
account of culling and destruction of birds. The Government of India will 
share costs of compensation on 50:50 basis with the State Governments. The 
present outbreak is localised to a lomited area of NavapurTaluka of 
Nandurbar District in Maharashtra, not in the entire Maharashtra. The 
containment operations will extend to cover some poultry in adjoining areas of 
Uchchhal Tehsil of Surat district in Gujarat 
State also. I would like to poi nt out that as per the WHO 
recommendations, poultry nd poultry products can be safely consumed if 
cooked at 70 degree Celsius in all parts of the food. 
I would like to assure the House and the public that t here is no cause for 
panic. The Government is keeping a close watch on the situation. Other 
States have Iso been alerted to remain vigilant. Thank You 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Now, statement by the Minister of Health and 
Family Welfare. As both the statements are on the same subject, 
clarifications will be taken up together, 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): Sir, the World Health Organisation (WHO) had issued an alert 
that Bird Flue could spread to other countries including India after an 
outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5N1) was first detected in the Republic of 
Korea in December, 2003. 
First, I would like to inform the House about our preparedness in this 
regard. The Ministry of Health and Family  Welfare, Government of India, took 
adequate measures to contain the human cases of Avian Influenza if it is to 
happen. A Joint Monitoring Group was set up on 27th January, 2004,-under 
the chairmanship of the Director General of Health Services, 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
which is reviewing the situation regular ly. A National Consultation Meeting on 
Pandemic Preparedness was taken by me on 1st August, 2005, with all 
stakeholders to discuss the influenza Pandemic Preparedness and Response 
Plan and after subsequent reviews, decision was taken for instituting 
interventions in a phased manner. 
Chief Secretaries of all States/Union Territories and Secretary, Department 
of Animal Husbandry were requested to keep a close watch on fatality among 
bird population, especially poultry and appearance of severe respiratory illness 
in the exposed human population and to inform any such occurrence to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Other Ministries like Home, Shipping, 
External Affairs, Environment and forests were also alerted. 
A contingency plan to manage human cases of Avian Influenza was 
prepared and circulated to all the States. A model State action plan was 
prepared and discussed with State Health  Secretaries. The National Institute 
of Communicable Diseases (NICD), Delhi, has been identified as the nodal 
agency to investigate' any suspected cases/outbreaks. National Institute of 
Virology '(NIV), Pune, was also identified for laboratory support. Rapid response 
teams were constituted and kept in readiness. Indian Council of Medical 
Research (ICMR) strengthened Influenza surveillance network. 
A task force under the chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) was constituted 
to ensure availability of drugs and vaccines for management of Avian Influenza 
in the country. This task force decided to procure one lakh courses of Oselta 
mivir(Tamiflu). Fifty thousand courses of Oseltamavir and 10,000 personal 
protective equipments: were stockpiled. 
NICD trained State level rapid response teams and held sensitisation 
workshops for para-military forces. In fact, Information, Education and 
Communication (IEC) strategies have also been finalised. 
Now, I would like to tell our response to the information of this virus. 
Information was received from the Department of Animal Husbandry about large-
scale mortality in poultry from Navapur taluk, Nsindurbar District of Maharashtra 
on 15th February, 2006. Preliminary reports had revealed the possibility of New 
Castle; (Ranikhet) disease. Further, the test reports of some samples from 
affected poultry were confirmed as positive for H5N1 strain of Avian Influenza on 
18th February, 2006. 
248 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
However, as a matter of abundant caution and without waiting for confirmation 
from High Security Aanimal Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal, Rapid Response 
Team (RRT) of NICD was deputed to Navapur, Maharashtra, on 16th February, 
2006, itself with all the necessary medicines and equipments. The team is presently 
surveying the area to identify the people who may have come in contact with the infected 
birds. 
On 17th February, the RRT visited the local hospitals and observed that over the 
last 10 days, there was no patient with common flu symptoms. However, subsequently, six 
persons with symptoms of common cold were detected and are under observation. 
None of these cases has any pneumonia. The teams are in the field and assisting 
the State health authorities in carrying out active surveillance (house-to-house search) to 
identify suspected cases among contacts of infected poultry. In order to make 
confirmatory tests, the RRT has obtained clinical samples randomly from the bird handlers 
and sent to NIV, Pune, and NICD, Delhi.  The samples are being tested as per 
protocols. Another RRT has been sent to Surat District, Gujarat on 19th February, 
2006. 
The Navapur sub-district hospital has been strengthened. Isolation beds have been 
created and dedicated staff identified for treating cases. Four ventilators have reached 
Navapur along with two anaesthetists. 
On 19th February, 2006, the Department of Animal Husbandry has started culling 
the birds as per their contingency plan. The RRT sensitised the cullers on proper use of 
personal protective equipments and self care. Health status of cullers is being 
monitored. 
My Ministry has dispatched 11,000 doses of Tamiflue and 3000 sets of Personal 
Protective Equipments to Maharashtra and Gujarat besides meeting the immediate 
requirement of Department of Animal Husbandry and is in constant touch with the State 
health authorities of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. Cabinet Secretary has 
also been reviewing the situation on regular basis. 
Round- the-clock control room is functioning from Emergency medical Relief Division, 
Directorate General of Health Services (Tel. No. 23061302; FAX: 23061457) and from 
National Institute of Communicable Diseases, 22, Sham Nath Marg (Tel. No: 
23921401; FAX 23913028). 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
As on date, there is no confirmed case  of human Avian influenza. I would 
like to assure the House that the situation is being Closely monitored and under 
control.

DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, nobody can control the pattern of 
migratory birds. Nobody can say whether these migratory birds will be here for 
three months, or, that they will go back after two-and-a-half months. It is their 
pattern. Sir, the hon. Minister of Agriculture will take up the other issues. Thank 
you. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, we got this particular 
information from a place called Navapur. Navapur is a tribal area. It is near to 
one major irrigation project called Kukai, and it is also one of the forest areas. 
And, as my colleague has just now mentioned, this type of disease is always 
carried by migratory birds; the major reason for it being nearer to the water area 
and, secondly, it is a forest area. There is every possibility that the birds coming 
from different parts might have brought this particular disease. But we have not 
come to any definite conclusion. Knowing about the area from where it has 
come, I thought I would give a little background. 
A mention was made by the hon. Member, Shri Joshi, about an 
advertisement which has appeared in today's newspapers published by the 
National AIDS Coordination Committee. Shrimati Arundhati Desai is the 
Chairperson of this particular organisation. The statement there says, "This is not 
a bird flu, but this is Ranikhet." Out initial information also was about Ranikhet. 
But when we sent these samples to a laboratory at Bhopal, which is fully 
equipped to test for Avian influenza, this laboratory has conducted a series of 
tests. Experts have analysed the processed used by this laboratory and found 
them to be credible.Their report is that 
263 

RAJYA SABHA [20 February, 2006] 
the samples are positive for Avian Influenza. This National AIDS Coordination 
Committee has mentioned the name of a particular expert, Dr. Kataria, who 
seemed to have said something. But, Dr. Kataria was one of the members 
who were deputed by the Government of India along with three other persons 
to visit Bhopal and to study each and every sample. All these four experts 
have given a written statement to the Go vernment of India saying that they 
had seen those samples and whatever procedure was adopted by the 
laboratory was correct, and that these are cases of Avian Influenza. So, 
whatever the Coordination Committee or  Shrimati Desai's statement which 
appeared on the media, could be a reaction to that, but the factual position is 
not that. The expert's report is altogether different, and that is the reasons why 
the Government of India has taken this particular problem very seriously. 
The second issue which was raised here is about culling of birds. As per 
the WHO guidelines, whenever any Government in the world gets any 
information about this Avian Influenza, it  is the responsibility of that local 
Government to take immediate action, and they have to destroy these birds 
within practically no time. We had discussed long back how we were going to 
protect the interests of the farmers, were something like this to happen. That 
is why a decision was taken that compensation would be paid, fifty per cent of 
which will come from the Government of India and fifty per cent will be 
contributed by the State Government. Th is particular decision was taken with 
the approval of the State Governments.  Whether it was Maharashtra or Tamil 
nadu, all State Governments had agreed to  this decision. It was decided that 
money will be made available to the St ate Governments for the payment of 
compensation to farmers. 
The hon. Member, Shri Ahluwalia, has raised the issue as to how we are 
going to dispose off the birds. जहां तक दफनाने की बात आपने कहीं, there are two 
ways; one is of burying and the other is of burning. It has to be ensured that 
disposal by burning is done in deep trenc hes; use of plastic sheets is to be 
done to cover the earth. We have reques ted the States of use JCBs. They 
can dig deep trenches. So, these are the types of steps that have been taken 
in Navapur, as per the WHO guidelines. 
A question was asked whether it were broi lers or layers. The extent of the 
death of broilers and layers will be k nown only finally, after the culling 
operation concludes. We are not studying whether they were broilers or 
264 

[20 February, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
layers. We can find out that later. Immediately, our effort is to dispose them off 
as early as possible. That is why we are taking that action. 
A question was asked about the sample s from Andhra Pradesh. No sample 
from Andhra Pradesh has tested positive for avian influenza. 
Sushmaji raised an issue, to which my colleague has already replied. This 
was regarding the media briefing. Daily media briefing is being done by the 
Department of Animal Husbandry and the Health Ministry. This particular 
briefing has been started from the 18th. 
The Government—whether it is the St ate Governments or the Government 
of India—had been taking this particular subject seriously since long. In fact, 
preparations for fighting this type of a problem had started, practically, four 
years ago in this country, in the respective State Governments, the Government 
of India, the Health Ministry and also in the respective Animal Husbandry 
Department of the Ministry of Agriculture. As my colleague has already mentioned, 
there were a series of meetings between the States and the Government of 
India. The entire machinery was put on alert. The Health Ministry was on alert. 
Then, the Animal Hus bandry departments in various States were also on alert. 
So, we had made all preparations to fight such a problem. 
I have an appeal to make, especially to the members of the media. My appeal 
is that they should not create panic. The truth is that this particular problem has 
erupted in a very limited area; it has been very localised. It is just in a three-to-ten 
kilometre area in a place called Navapur. Till today, we have not got any 
information of its going beyond that three-to-ten kilometre area. That is why we 
are concentrating on that particular area. We have taken such steps that it does 
not spread to other parts of the State and the country.  So, it is not a problem 
that has erupted in the entire country. The reports which have appeared in the 
media, especially in the electronic medi a, are indicating that this problem 
seems to be there throughout India. I am sorry this is not a problem that is 
there throughout India. 
The only thing is that one has to take this particular industry very seriously. 
Sir, this particular industry is practically worth Rs. 35,000 crores. It is not a small 
industry. It has an annual growth rate of 17 per cent. This is one of the growing 
industries in the country and it provides a lot of jobs.

More than three million people are already involved in this industry and a majority 
of them are in the rural area s. That is why it is all the more important that we 
protect the interests of this industry and the interests of the farming community. If 
something goes wrong, we will take all possible steps. But we should not create an 
atmosphere as if the entire industry is affected and as if eating an egg or a 
chicken is a dangerous thing. That is not the case. As I have already mentioned, 
as per the WHO guidelines, if we boil an egg or a chicken at 70 degrees, it will 
not be harmful for anybody. So, those types of guidelines have been 
communicated by the WHO and we would also like to communicate the same 
to the entire country.
